content: The Fischer-Tropsch process is a chemical reaction that uses catalysts to convert carbon monoxide and hydrogen into liquid hydrocarbons of various forms. Common catalysts for this process are based on iron and cobalt. The primary goal of the Fischer-Tropsch process is to produce synthetic petroleum substitutes, often derived from coal or natural gas, which can be used as synthetic lubrication oil or synthetic fuel. The carbon monoxide and hydrogen required for this process can be generated through other reactions, such as the partial combustion of hydrocarbons (e.g., methane in gas-to-liquid applications) or the gasification of coal or biomass. The energy required for the endothermic reaction of coal or biomass with steam is typically supplied by exothermic combustion with air or oxygen. The mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen produced is referred to as synthesis gas or syngas. The hydrocarbon products resulting from the Fischer-Tropsch process are refined to create the desired synthetic fuels. Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are generated during the partial oxidation of coal and wood-based fuels. The process is particularly useful for producing liquid hydrocarbons from solid feedstocks, such as coal or solid carbon-containing wastes. Non-oxidative pyrolysis of solid materials can also produce syngas, which can be used directly as a fuel without undergoing Fischer-Tropsch transformations. However, if liquid petroleum-like fuels, lubricants, or waxes are required, the Fischer-Tropsch process is applied. The Fischer-Tropsch process was originally developed in the 1920s by German researchers Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute. It was invented in Germany, a country rich in coal but poor in petroleum, to produce liquid fuels. During World War II, Germany and Japan used the process to produce ersatz fuels, with Germany producing 5 million tons in 1944. After the war, German scientists captured during Operation Paperclip continued working on synthetic fuels in the United States under a program initiated by the Synthetic Liquid Fuels Act. Currently, only a few companies have commercialized Fischer-Tropsch technology. Shell operates a plant in Bintulu, Malaysia, using natural gas as a feedstock to produce low-sulfur diesel fuels and food-grade wax. Sasol in South Africa uses coal and natural gas as feedstocks to produce a variety of synthetic petroleum products, including most of the country’s diesel fuel. Sasol employed the process during South Africa’s isolation under Apartheid to meet its energy needs. The process has gained renewed attention for producing low-sulfur diesel fuel to reduce the environmental impact of diesel engines. A U.S.-based company, Rentech, is focusing on converting nitrogen-fertilizer plants from natural gas feedstocks to coal or coke, producing liquid hydrocarbons as a by-product. Other companies, such as Choren Industries in Germany, Changing World Technologies (CWT), and the GTL Corporation, have also built Fischer-Tropsch plants or use similar processes. The GTL Corporation employs a micro-GTL process, which is compact and can be used directly at natural gas well sites. Two micro-GTL pilot plants have been successfully tested in Oklahoma. The Fischer-Tropsch process is an established technology already applied on a large scale. However, its widespread adoption is limited by high capital costs, high operation and maintenance costs, and the volatile price of crude oil. The process is particularly suited for exploiting stranded gas reserves—natural gas sources located far from major cities, which are impractical to exploit using conventional gas pipelines or LNG technology. Several companies are working to develop the process for practical exploitation of these reserves. Geologists predict that natural gas supplies will peak 5–15 years after oil does, although such predictions are uncertain. Large coal reserves may increasingly be used as a fuel source during oil depletion. Given the abundance of coal reserves worldwide, this technology could serve as an interim transportation fuel solution if conventional oil becomes more expensive. Combining biomass gasification (BG) with Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis is a promising route for producing renewable or green transportation fuels. In September 2005, Pennsylvania Governor Edward Rendell announced a venture to build a Fischer-Tropsch plant that would convert waste coal into low-sulfur diesel fuel. The project, located outside Mahanoy City, Pennsylvania, uses technology licensed from Shell and Sasol. The U.S. Department of Energy has offered over $140 million in tax incentives for the project. Other coal-producing states are exploring similar plans. For example, Montana Governor Brian Schweitzer has proposed a plant to convert the state’s coal reserves into fuel using the Fischer-Tropsch process, aiming to reduce U.S. dependence on foreign oil. In October 2006, Finnish paper and pulp manufacturer UPM announced plans to produce biodiesel using the Fischer-Tropsch process alongside its European paper and pulp manufacturing operations. The process would utilize waste biomass from paper and pulp production as a source material. In August 2007, Louisiana State University received funding from the U.S. Department of Energy and ConocoPhillips to develop new nanotechnologies for catalyzing coal syngas into ethanol. Syntroleum, a publicly traded U.S. company, has produced over 400,000 gallons of diesel and jet fuel using the Fischer-Tropsch process at its demonstration plant near Tulsa, Oklahoma. The company is working to commercialize its proprietary Fischer-Tropsch technology through coal-to-liquid plants in the U.S., China, and Germany, as well as gas-to-liquid plants internationally. Using natural gas as a feedstock, the ultra-clean, low-sulfur fuel has been extensively tested by the U.S. Department of Energy, the Department of Transportation, and the U.S. Air Force. Syntroleum has collaborated with the U.S. Air Force to develop a synthetic jet fuel blend to reduce dependence on imported petroleum. In December 2006, a B-52 aircraft successfully completed a seven-hour flight powered by a 50-50 blend of JP-8 and Fischer-Tropsch fuel. The Air Force aims to certify all aircraft in its inventory to use the fuel by 2011. Environmental concerns regarding the Fischer-Tropsch process include the significant increase in primary energy use and carbon emissions associated with converting gaseous and solid carbon sources into liquid fuels. This is particularly problematic if the energy used to drive the process comes from burning coal or hydrocarbon fuels. Research by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory indicates that full fuel cycle greenhouse gas emissions for coal-based synthetic fuels are nearly twice as high as their petroleum-based equivalents. Emissions of other pollutants are also significantly increased, although many of these emissions can be captured during production. Carbon sequestration has been proposed as a mitigation strategy for greenhouse gas emissions, but its adoption is limited without a carbon tax or emissions cap. Biomass gasification technology offers a carbon-neutral alternative. Biomass-powered synthetic fuel plants are considered one of the most promising energy solutions for a carbon-neutral economy. Hybrid hydrogen-carbon processes have also been proposed as a closed-carbon cycle alternative, combining clean electricity, recycled CO, H2, and captured CO2 with biomass inputs to reduce the amount of biomass needed.
